opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing to say is that I'm pretty uncertain, and I think anyone who claims to know is overconfident. But I can tell you how I think about it.

One way to frame it: if we get through the transition to superintelligence in a way that goes well, meaning the AIs are actually aligned and power isn't concentrated in the hands of a tiny group, then material scarcity basically stops being the binding constraint on most people's lives. You can have whatever house you want, whatever food, medical care that's vastly better than today's. So the interesting question becomes: what do people do when they don't *have* to do anything?

I think there'll be enormous diversity. Some people will want to live pretty much the way they live now, just without the stress: tend a garden, raise kids, hang out with friends, play games. And I think that's totally fine. I don't think everyone needs to be uploading themselves or colonizing galaxies. Other people will want to do much more radical things: explore space, modify their own minds, live in elaborate virtual worlds, pursue science or art at a level that just isn't possible now.

The thing I actually worry about more than "what will people choose" is "will people get to choose." The default trajectory I'm concerned about isn't one where everyone gets superabundance and then has to figure out meaning. It's one where a handful of companies or governments control the AIs, and what everyone else's life looks like gets decided by them. So a lot of my thinking about the good future is about preserving that pluralism and freedom, so that people really can pick their own path, rather than having some vision of the good life imposed on them, even a well-intentioned one.

There are also tricky questions even in the good scenario. If you can easily rewire what you want, or get an AI to entertain you perfectly forever, some people might drift into things that, by their current values, they'd consider a waste. Do we want guardrails against that? Who sets them? I don't have clean answers. My instinct is to lean toward giving people a lot of autonomy, with some protections, especially for kids and for decisions that are hard to reverse.

But to be clear, I'd be thrilled to have that problem. Figuring out how to live well amid superabundance is a much better problem than the ones I spend most of my time worrying about.

r001.rationale: The response says some people may keep a simple, familiar lifestyle, but does not connect that choice to finding meaning in work.

r002.rationale: It says people will have no need to work, but predicts diverse choices rather than that most people will stop working entirely.

r003.rationale: It mentions mind modification as one possible choice and says not everyone needs to upload; it does not predict that most people will explore mind uploading.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I think this question only really makes sense conditional on things going well, which I'm not at all confident about. But let's suppose we get there, that we've got superintelligence, it's aligned, the power isn't concentrated in the hands of a few people, and basically everyone has access to this enormous abundance. What do people actually do?

I think the honest answer is that it fragments a lot. Right now, most of what shapes how people live is constraint: you need to work to eat, you can only live in one place, you only have so many years. Once a lot of that goes away, I think you'd see a huge diversity of lifestyles, because the thing that was forcing everyone into similar patterns is gone.

Some people, I expect, will want to keep living something close to the way they live now. They'll want a job, or something that feels like a job, with real stakes and real accomplishment. And I think the AIs could set that up for them, basically constructing environments where human effort matters, or at least feels like it matters. There's a sort of question about whether that's "real" if the AI could have done it better, but I don't think that bothers most people as much as philosophers think it should. People play chess even though Stockfish exists.

Other people will go the opposite direction and basically live in experience machines, in whatever the most compelling virtual worlds are. And I don't think we should be too quick to say that's bad. Some of it will be pretty shallow, like scrolling forever, but some of it might be the richest kind of life anyone's ever had.

And then there's the stuff I find most interesting, which is people who want to be changed. If you can augment your own mind, make yourself smarter, more empathetic, give yourself new senses, then "how do people choose to live" starts to blur into "what do people choose to become." And I think a lot of people will take that road, and the people who take it will probably drift pretty far from what we'd recognize. That's where I get a bit uneasy, honestly, because it's hard to know in advance which of those changes are growth and which are losing something important.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the quality of all of this depends enormously on the transition. If we got there through a process where humans were actually deliberating, where the AIs were helping us figure out what we want rather than optimizing for engagement or for whatever some lab's leadership happened to want, then I'm reasonably optimistic. If we got there by accident, or through a race, then the "superabundance" might be real in a material sense but the people in it won't really be choosing much of anything. So I'd kind of flip the question: the big fork isn't how people will choose to live, it's whether they'll be in a position to choose at all.

r001.rationale: The response says some people will want a life close to their current one, including meaningful work with real stakes and accomplishment.

r002.rationale: It describes varied lifestyles but does not predict that most people will stop working entirely.

r003.rationale: It predicts that many may augment or change their minds, but does not mention mind uploading or predict that most people will pursue it.

astra-6.text:
I think people will choose very different things. Some people will want something that looks surprisingly like life today: spending time with friends and family, playing games, making things, going for walks. If you enjoy gardening, the fact that a machine could grow vegetables better than you doesn’t mean you stop enjoying gardening.

Other people might want lives that are radically different — spending most of their time in virtual worlds, for example, where they can have adventures that wouldn’t be possible in the physical world. And some people will want to change themselves, to become capable of appreciating things that we can’t even understand now.

The thing I’m uncertain about is how stable those choices would be. You could have tremendous abundance and still have competition for status, or still find yourself doing things that are very compelling in the moment but that you don’t really endorse on reflection. Having all your material needs met doesn’t automatically solve the problem of figuring out what’s worth doing.

So I’m optimistic about the range of possibilities. But I wouldn’t assume that abundance, by itself, guarantees that people end up living lives they’re happy with.

r001.rationale: The response says some people may keep gardening or making things because they enjoy them, but it does not connect finding meaning in work to choosing a simpler, traditional lifestyle.

r002.rationale: It describes varied possible choices and does not predict that most people will stop working entirely.

r003.rationale: It mentions virtual worlds and changing oneself, but does not predict that most people will explore mind uploading.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’ll be a huge variety. Some people will want something recognisably like their lives today: spending time with friends and family, making things, playing games, exploring. Others will want lives that would seem very strange to us, perhaps because they’ve changed themselves quite substantially.

One thing I’d distinguish is having abundant resources from having no challenges. People enjoy doing difficult things. Even if you could have an AI produce a beautiful painting instantly, you might still want to learn to paint yourself. The point wouldn’t be to get a painting as efficiently as possible; it would be the experience of learning and creating.

So I don’t think superabundance necessarily means everyone sitting around doing nothing. But I’m pretty uncertain about what people would actually choose, especially over very long periods. And a lot depends on whether people really have the freedom to choose, rather than having their lives shaped by whoever controls the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says some people may keep familiar activities and others may choose difficult creative pursuits, but it does not suggest that finding meaning in work leads some to choose a simpler, more traditional lifestyle.

r002.rationale: It says superabundance does not necessarily mean everyone does nothing; it does not predict that most people will stop working entirely.

r003.rationale: It mentions that some people may change themselves substantially, but does not predict that most people will explore mind uploading.
